input_signals.name: Externally_Financed_Intangible_Buildup
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), at), 1)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Balance-sheet intangibles and goodwill grow mainly through acquisitions, so a jump in recorded intangibles that coincides with heavy simultaneous equity and debt issuance identifies externally financed empire building and overpayment rather than organic innovation.
input_signals.reasoning: The product of two within-industry ranks fires only when both intangible-asset expansion and gross external financing are high, isolating acquirers who paid with freshly raised (often overvalued) capital. Such firms face subsequent write-down risk and issuance-related underperformance, which neither the intangible-growth nor the issuance leg captures alone.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( delta( ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Payout_Funded_RD_Expansion
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), at), 1)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, ADD(sstk, dltis)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that expand intangible investment intensity while simultaneously returning capital (repurchases exceeding new equity and debt issuance) are funding innovation entirely from internal cash flow, revealing both cash-flow strength and managerial conviction that the shares are cheap; this joint corner is the cleanest identification of productive, non-market-timed intangible financing.
input_signals.reasoning: This keeps the winning economic channel from gen-0 (`RD_Commitment_Under_Financing_Withdrawal`, FF5 alpha 2.5%, t=2.73) but replaces the winsorized z-score product — whose fat tails left fmb_tstat at 0.36 — with a product of bounded non-negative within-industry ranks, which should linearize the cross-sectional slope without destroying the sort. Using net-payout level rather than its first difference also stabilizes portfolio composition, since one-year financing changes are noisy and cause turnover in the extreme legs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( delta( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( prstkc, add( sstk, dltis ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt_Paydown_By_Intangible_Innovators
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Innovation-intensive firms that are net repaying long-term debt are generating enough internal cash to both fund research and shrink fixed claims, which lowers the deadweight cost of holding non-pledgeable intangible capital; the credit market, unlike the equity market, cannot be timed, so debt reduction by an R&D-intensive firm is a cash-flow fact rather than a valuation signal.
input_signals.reasoning: Gen-0 evidence that debt-financed R&D earned a mildly negative alpha motivates testing the opposite credit-market state — deleveraging — through a financing instrument (dltr minus dltis) entirely separate from the equity payout channel, so it is not a restatement of the stock-financed-acquirer or issuance anomalies. Scaling R&D by sales rather than assets measures research intensity relative to the revenue base it must eventually support, and the three-year average keeps the conditioning leg slow-moving for stable portfolio composition.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( dltr, dltis ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Sustained_Selffunded_Innovation_Trend
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), at), 5)), IND_RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is the multi-year trajectory, not a single fiscal year: firms on a five-year upward path of intangible investment intensity while their reliance on external capital markets is simultaneously trending down are progressively internalizing the funding of innovation, a durable state the market prices too slowly.
input_signals.reasoning: The alpha-versus-slope disagreement in the archive's per-share intangible signal pointed to a noisy, tail-driven one-year growth construction, so this replaces event-year changes with two five-year trend slopes, a genuinely different temporal object that is smooth, slow-moving and therefore better suited to both a linear cross-sectional slope and stable long-short legs. Interacting the two trajectories (rather than differencing two anomaly ranks) means the signal fires only for firms whose innovation ramp and financing-independence ramp coincide.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( trend( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), at ), 5 ) ), ind_rank( neg( trend( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Brand_Capital_Built_Without_Dilution
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xad, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Advertising builds customer capital that is fully expensed and therefore invisible on the balance sheet, and that hidden asset accrues to existing shareholders only if the share count is not expanding; brand-intensive firms with shrinking share counts concentrate unrecognized customer capital per share, while brand-intensive diluters transfer it to new investors.
input_signals.reasoning: Advertising is essentially unexplored in the archive and is economically distinct from R&D — customer capital depreciates faster and is financed almost entirely from operating cash flow — so this tests whether the funding-source mechanism generalizes beyond research capital. The signed dilution leg ensures brand-intensive firms occupy both extreme legs (repurchasers versus diluters), keeping the test orthogonal to the level of advertising intensity itself.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xad, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( neg( growth( csho, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Internal_Coverage_Gap_Funding_Choice
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(xrd, ADD(xrd, ABS(SUB(revt, cogs))))), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The productive-versus-opportunistic financing distinction bites hardest where current operations cannot cover the research bill: among firms whose R&D is large relative to gross profit, those that still avoid net external capital are funding the gap from accumulated internal resources and genuine conviction, while those closing the gap with fresh issuance are dependent on market sentiment.
input_signals.reasoning: The flagged version's burn leg was effectively negated gross profitability in levels; replacing it with the bounded share xrd/(xrd + |gross profit|) removes that scale domination and makes it a pure internal-coverage ratio used only as a non-negative conditioning weight. The financing leg is now signed net external financing, so the hypothesis is internally consistent across both tails — high-coverage-gap net payers long, high-coverage-gap net absorbers short — with low-gap firms carrying little weight either way.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( xrd, add( xrd, abs( sub( revt, cogs ) ) ) ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Purchased_Versus_Organic_Use_Of_Raised_Capital
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), at), 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters about externally raised capital is what it buys: firms that channel raised funds into purchased intangibles and goodwill are paying market prices for other people's innovation and are prone to overpayment, while firms whose raised funds show up as expanded in-house research are building capital at cost; the same total financing therefore predicts opposite outcomes depending on the intangible channel it feeds.
input_signals.reasoning: This resolves rather than labels the tension the critic identified: the sign is attached to the *composition* of intangible expansion (purchased minus organic) conditional on heavy financing, so it does not assert that falling intangibles are bad, and it is not post-impairment drift. Both extreme legs are three-year heavy external financiers, differing only in whether the money went into acquisitions or into R&D, which keeps the test orthogonal to the issuance and asset-growth main effects that the archive's financed-buildup signal already captured.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ts_sum( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), at ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( sub( delta( ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), at ), 1 ), delta( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), at ), 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Multiyear_Deleveraging_Innovators
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(TS_SUM(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), 3), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Sustained net repayment of long-term debt by a research-intensive firm is a multi-year cash-flow fact that cannot be timed or window-dressed: it shows the innovation program is throwing off enough cash to shrink fixed claims, while research-intensive firms cumulatively drawing down credit are financing intangibles with claims their assets cannot collateralize.
input_signals.reasoning: `Debt_Paydown_By_Intangible_Innovators` was the only archive signal with same-signed, non-trivial evidence on both metrics (fmb 2.0; alpha 1.6%, t 1.9), so it deserves consolidation rather than abandonment; replacing its second non-negative rank with a signed industry z-score gives the sort a real short leg (research-intensive net borrowers) instead of a diffuse one. Cumulating the debt flow over three years converts a lumpy annual financing item into a persistent state, which should raise both the slope precision and portfolio stability.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( sub( dltr, dltis ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Maturity_Mismatch_On_Intangible_Assets
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3)), at)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, dltt)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Intangible assets pay off over long, uncertain horizons and cannot be liquidated to meet a near-term maturity, so intangible-intensive firms that fund themselves with a high share of short-term debt bear rollover risk that can force premature abandonment of research programs; the same short-maturity structure is largely harmless for a tangible-asset firm that can borrow against collateral.
input_signals.reasoning: Debt maturity structure is a financing dimension untouched by the archive — prior leverage tests used the level or the one-year change, which overlap the asset-growth and debt-issuance anomalies, whereas the short-term share of debt is roughly orthogonal to leverage magnitude. The signed maturity leg (negated, so long leg is intangible-intensive long-maturity financing and short leg is intangible-intensive short-maturity financing) again places intangible-heavy firms at both extremes, insulating the test from the R&D-level effect that has been inflating alphas elsewhere in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ) ), at ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( dlc, add( dlc, dltt ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Hidden_Equity_Behind_Repurchases
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), ADD(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), ABS(ceq)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: For firms whose accumulated research spending is large relative to reported book equity, the balance sheet understates capital most severely, so conventional valuation screens misclassify them; when such a firm is also retiring its own shares rather than selling them, insiders are buying an asset the accounting system does not show, and the market's slow recognition of that hidden equity produces excess returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Every earlier self-funding test scaled intangible spending by assets, which conflates size with mismeasurement; scaling five-year cumulative R&D by itself-plus-book-equity gives a bounded index of how badly book value is understated, which is the actual economic reason financing decisions are informative here. The signed net-equity-payout leg puts the most mismeasured firms at both extremes — repurchasers versus diluters — so the test does not simply recover the repurchase or R&D-to-equity main effects.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), add( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), abs( ceq ) ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Financing_Without_Pricing_Power
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 3))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross margin is the visible rent on a firm's intangible capital — brands, process know-how, switching costs — so a firm with thin margins has little intangible advantage to scale; external capital absorbed by such a firm buys commodity capacity and is value-destroying, whereas capital returned by a thin-margin firm signals discipline about a business that should not grow.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the industry-mean moderator (which the critic correctly showed was algebraically the previously tested one) with a firm-level measure of realized intangible rents that no archive signal has used, and it is not a restatement of R&D intensity since low-margin firms are typically the non-innovators. Both tails are thin-margin firms differing only in financing direction, so the interaction — not the net-financing main effect — determines which extreme leg a firm enters.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), revt ), 3 ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Innovation_Funding_Under_Revenue_Stress
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MUL(NEG(GROWTH(sale, 1)), MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3))), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Adversity reveals type: when revenue is contracting at a research-intensive firm, the funding source becomes maximally diagnostic, because only firms with genuine internal resources and confidence in their pipeline can keep investing while returning or at least not absorbing outside capital, whereas the stressed innovator that leans on the market is financing survival on sentiment.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a state-dependence mechanism rather than another temporal statistic of issuance — the claim is that the informativeness of financing direction is concentrated in the stressed-innovator state, which no archive signal has conditioned on. The weight is a composite stress-and-intensity state and the signed leg is financing direction, so the extreme legs are both stressed research-intensive firms and the sort is not driven by revenue growth or issuance alone.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( mul( neg( growth( sale, 1 ) ), ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparty_Funded_Innovation
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Not all outside funding comes from capital markets: growth in non-debt liabilities — supplier credit, customer prepayments, deferred revenue — is financing extended by informed commercial counterparties who can observe a research program's progress directly, so an intangible-intensive firm whose operating-liability funding is expanding has been validated by parties with private information, whereas one whose counterparty funding is shrinking is losing the confidence of the people closest to its products.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the mismeasurement/net-repurchase family entirely and introduces a financing source the archive has never used — liabilities net of interest-bearing debt — which is informationally distinct from arms-length issuance because trade creditors and customers monitor the product, not the stock price. Both extreme legs are research-intensive firms split by the direction of counterparty funding, so neither the R&D-intensity nor the issuance main effect determines leg membership.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Purchased_Intangible_Base_Financing
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), ADD(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose intangible capital was bought rather than built has already paid market prices for other people's innovation, and continuing to absorb outside capital in that state funds a treadmill of further acquisitions at fair or inflated prices; the same purchased-intangible profile combined with net capital return signals an acquirer that has stopped rolling the dice and is harvesting.
input_signals.reasoning: The moderator is the *composition* of the existing intangible stock — purchased goodwill as a share of goodwill plus accumulated research — which is a bounded balance-sheet characteristic no archive signal has used, unlike the earlier test that put intangible growth *flows* in the signed leg. Both tails consist of acquisition-built firms differing in financing direction, so the interaction rather than goodwill intensity or net financing alone drives the sort.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( coalesce( gdwl, 0 ), add( coalesce( gdwl, 0 ), ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ) ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparty_Versus_Market_Funding_Mix
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), ADD(sstk, dltis)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: For a research-intensive firm the informative comparison is which set of financiers is supplying the marginal dollar: commercial counterparties who observe the products and the pipeline directly, or arms-length investors who observe only the share price; firms funding innovation through expanding operating liabilities while taking little from capital markets have been validated by informed parties, and the reverse configuration is financing on sentiment.
input_signals.reasoning: This extends the archive's best joint-evidence signal from a single funding source to the *mix* of informed versus arms-length funding, which is the economic content of the mechanism rather than a smoothing knob, and it means the short leg is now explicitly capital-market-funded innovators rather than merely firms with flat operating liabilities. Both tails remain research-intensive, so the sort is driven by funding provenance rather than by R&D intensity or issuance levels.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), 1 ), add( sstk, dltis ) ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Hidden_Equity_Meets_Counterparty_Funding
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), ADD(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), ABS(ceq)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The firms most severely mismeasured by accounting — those whose accumulated research dwarfs reported book equity — are exactly the firms outside investors cannot value, so evidence from informed commercial counterparties should matter most for them: expanding trade and customer financing tells the market that the invisible asset is real, while contracting counterparty funding is the earliest signal that it is not.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the archive's strongest slope-producing moderator (mismeasurement index, fmb 5.3) with its strongest alpha-producing financing leg (counterparty funding change, alpha t 2.9), a combination justified by the mechanism — mismeasurement is precisely the condition under which informed-party validation carries incremental information — rather than by statistics alone. Because the moderator is bounded and the financing leg is a signed asset-scaled change, both tails are populated mismeasured firms split by counterparty behaviour.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), add( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), abs( ceq ) ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparty_Funding_Of_Brand_Capital
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xad, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Customer capital built through advertising is validated by the commercial channel before it is visible in earnings: expanding trade credit and customer prepayments at an advertising-intensive firm mean distributors and buyers are committing their own money to the brand, while contracting counterparty funding means the channel is pulling back even if reported sales have not yet fallen.
input_signals.reasoning: This tests whether the counterparty-financing mechanism — the archive's only two-sided result — generalizes from research capital to brand capital, where the informed counterparties are distributors and customers rather than technology partners, using a largely disjoint industry population. A confirming result would establish the mechanism as being about informed-party funding rather than about R&D firms specifically; a null would sharply narrow its interpretation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xad, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparty_Verdict_On_Acquired_Intangibles
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a firm's asset base is largely purchased goodwill, the honest test of whether the acquisitions bought real businesses is whether the customers and suppliers of those businesses keep committing their own money: expanding trade credit and customer prepayments confirm the acquired operations are healthy, while contracting counterparty funding is the earliest, pre-impairment evidence that the price paid will not be recovered.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the net-external-financing leg the critic identified as a repackaged anomaly and instead applies the archive's only two-sided mechanism — informed-counterparty funding — to the acquisition-built population, where accounting value is least verifiable and impairments arrive with a long lag. It is a genuine economic test rather than a moderator-denominator variant: goodwill intensity determines whose verdict we are reading, and the signed counterparty leg puts acquisition-heavy firms at both tails with broad coverage.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( coalesce( gdwl, 0 ), at ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparty_Support_Streak_Innovators
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 0), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: One year of expanding trade credit can be a working-capital accident; four or five consecutive years of it means the commercial ecosystem has repeatedly renewed its willingness to fund a research-intensive firm, which is the durable version of informed-party validation and the version that should be priced slowly.
input_signals.reasoning: A count of expansion years is a magnitude-free statistic, so it cannot be the operating-accrual effect in disguise — the accrual anomaly is about the size of the accrual, not the number of years its sign was positive — making this the cleanest available discriminating test of the mechanism. The same count functional form was judged the archive's most credible novel construction, and here it is applied to the one financing source that has produced two-sided evidence.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( ts_sum( indicator( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Market_Funding_Replacing_Counterparty_Support
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1)), 0), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The damaging configuration is substitution: when suppliers and customers pull back their funding from a research-intensive firm and the gap is plugged with fresh capital-market money, the firm is replacing informed capital with uninformed capital, which is what a manager does when the people closest to the business have already decided the program is failing.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive tested the mirror state (issuance while counterparty funding was *expanding*, i.e. unnecessary issuance) and found little, which is informative: redundancy is weak evidence but substitution should be strong, because it identifies capital raised against a deteriorating informed-party assessment. The indicator restricts the issuance measure to contraction years so the extreme short leg is a specific economic event rather than the issuance level.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( mul( indicator( neg( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ) ), 0 ), ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), at ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparties_Follow_The_Research_Ramp
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(LAG(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 1), 1), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A research ramp is a claim about future products; the test of that claim is whether the commercial ecosystem funds it in the following year, since suppliers extending terms and customers prepaying after a firm has visibly increased its research effort are ratifying the program with their own money, while an unfunded ramp is an unvalidated one.
input_signals.reasoning: The conditioning variable is the *lagged* research ramp rather than the intangible-intensity level, so both tails consist of recent R&D expanders separated by the subsequent counterparty verdict, which makes this a sequencing test rather than another scaling of the parent signal. The archive already ran the arms-length version of this sequencing idea (issuance following a research ramp, alpha 1.4%, t 1.4); running it with informed rather than uninformed capital directly tests whose money constitutes validation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( lag( delta( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 1 ), 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Ramp_Validated_By_Informed_Money
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(LAG(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 1), 1), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), ADD(sstk, dltis)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that visibly increased research intensity last year has made a claim about future products; the following year reveals who paid for it, and the good outcome is that commercial counterparties funded the ramp while capital markets were not tapped, whereas the bad outcome is a ramp underwritten by share and bond sales with no commercial commitment behind it.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two strongest configurations — the lagged-ramp moderator (alpha +2.5%, t 3.05, sharpe 0.34) and the informed-versus-arms-length funding mix (fmb 4.20, alpha +2.7%, t 3.22) — but unlike a statistical recombination the join is the mechanism itself: sequencing establishes what the money was for, and the mix establishes who supplied it. Both tails are recent research rampers, separated by funding provenance.

input_signals.name: Acquisitions_Ratified_By_Counterparties
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(LAG(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), at), 1), 1), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: An acquisition is a bet that purchased intangible capital is worth what was paid, and the first independent verdict arrives from the acquired business's own customers and suppliers: if they expand prepayments and trade terms in the year after the deal, the operations are healthy, while flat or shrinking counterparty funding is pre-impairment evidence that the price will not be recovered.
input_signals.reasoning: The sequencing structure that worked for organic research ramps is applied here to purchased intangibles, a largely disjoint population and the one where accounting value is least verifiable and impairment lags longest, making it a genuine extension rather than a moderator swap. It also connects the archive's two independent counterparty results (organic ramp validation, alpha +2.5%; goodwill-intensity moderator, alpha +2.0%) into a single dynamic test of whether acquisitions get ratified.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( lag( delta( ratio( coalesce( gdwl, 0 ), at ), 1 ), 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Payout_Flexibility_Persistence_Innovators
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at), 0), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Financial flexibility is a policy, not a transaction: a research-intensive firm that in most of the last five years returned more cash through repurchases than through dividends has deliberately avoided committing to a rigid distribution, preserving the ability to keep funding research when cash flow disappoints, whereas an innovator that consistently leans on dividends has bound itself to a claim that must be honoured before the pipeline.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the t-stat-motivated blend and instead reimplements a single mechanism — payout rigidity versus flexibility, which produced a 2.4% alpha and the archive's best sharpe (0.39) but no slope — with the magnitude-free count form that has repeatedly fixed skew domination in this archive. Counting policy years rather than measuring dollar differences removes the lumpy-buyback outliers that most plausibly flattened the cross-sectional slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( ts_sum( indicator( ratio( sub( prstkc, dvt ), at ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparty_Support_Despite_Revenue_Decline
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(GROWTH(sale, 1)), 0), MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Expanding trade credit and customer prepayments during a year of *falling* revenue cannot be a mechanical consequence of business volume — it is a deliberate decision by suppliers and customers to increase their exposure to a research-intensive firm whose sales are shrinking, which is the strongest possible informed-party endorsement of a pipeline the income statement has not yet vindicated.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a state-dependence claim rather than another scaling of the counterparty leg, and it is the sharpest available test against the operating-accrual and liability-growth explanations, because in the conditioning sample the mechanical link between activity and operating liabilities runs the wrong way. The weight is nonzero only for shrinking research-intensive firms, so both extreme legs sit inside that stressed population and the sort is not driven by growth, size or issuance.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( mul( indicator( neg( growth( sale, 1 ) ), 0 ), ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparty_Support_By_Industry_Intangibility
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), IND_ADJ(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The same balance-sheet movement means opposite things in different technological environments: in a knowledge-intensive industry, growing operating liabilities are customers prepaying and partners committing to an unverifiable pipeline, while in a commodity industry they are more often stretched payables at a firm conserving cash, so the interaction should be with the industry's intangibility rather than with the individual firm's spending.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces threshold tuning on a firm-level gate with a continuous industry-level moderator, which resolves the population question without the coverage and composition shift the critic identified, since every firm retains a weight and none is deleted. The moderator is an environment characteristic recovered from the industry mean, so a positive result cannot be a firm-level R&D-intensity reweighting of the operating-liability effect.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), ind_adj( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ) ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Delayed_Market_Funding_After_Withdrawal
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(LAG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)), 0), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Substitution is a response that takes time: when commercial counterparties withdraw funding from a research-intensive firm in one year and the firm goes to the capital markets in the *following* year, management is replacing informed capital with uninformed capital after having seen the informed verdict, which is the clearest evidence that the raise is not demand-driven financing.
input_signals.reasoning: Using the lagged counterparty contraction as the gate breaks the mechanical dependence the critic identified — the current-year operating-liability change no longer appears in the expression, so the sign cannot be a reweighted flip of the established contemporaneous counterparty effect — and it makes substitution an identifiable sequence rather than a contemporaneous correlation. Both tails are research-intensive firms that lost counterparty support last year, separated by how aggressively they turned to the market this year.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( mul( indicator( neg( lag( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ), 1 ) ), 0 ), ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), at ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Commercial_Support_Drawdown
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), TS_MAX(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 5)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Commercial financing relationships are sticky, so what matters is how far a research-intensive firm's counterparty funding has fallen below the peak level its own suppliers and customers once extended: a firm sitting at its five-year high of commercial support retains full ecosystem confidence, while one deep below its own peak has suffered a cumulative withdrawal that annual changes can mask if the decline was spread over several years.
input_signals.reasoning: Distance-from-peak is a cumulative-erosion statistic distinct from the change, level, own-history rank and expansion count already tested, and it captures multi-year withdrawal that one-year differences and rank positions both miss. It also avoids the degenerate mass problems of the earlier own-history construction because the drawdown is a continuous magnitude, zero only for firms currently at their peak.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( sub( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), ts_max( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Shrinking_Intangibles_Confirmed_By_Counterparties
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), at), 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a firm's recorded intangible base is shrinking through amortisation, write-downs or divestiture, the open question is whether the underlying businesses are still healthy; if suppliers and customers are simultaneously reducing their funding, two independent parties are confirming deterioration, whereas continued commercial support says the accounting decline overstates the economic one.
input_signals.reasoning: The moderator is intangible-base *contraction*, a state the archive has only ever tested in expansion form (financed buildup, goodwill increases), so this examines the opposite half of the intangible life cycle where accounting value and economic value diverge most. Both tails consist of firms whose intangible base is shrinking, separated by whether the commercial ecosystem corroborates the write-down, which makes the sort a corroboration test rather than an impairment-drift rediscovery.
